### **q1** Planning a study (TEAMWORK)

While you provided this plan in c08 (Part 1), please include your plan here. In particular, describe how you updated your plan in response to feedback.

#### Population

- (What population are you going to study?)
  - All of the Islanders? Only the residents of Helvig? Participants meeting certain criteria (in which case, you need to list *covariates*)?
- We are studying the populations of Colmar, Mahuti, Gordes, and Valais. We will only be looking at people who have jobs.

#### Quantity of interest

- Percentage of people who are satisfied with their job depending on the size of town they live in.

#### Covariates

- Age
- Salary
- Job

#### Observation or experiment?

The Islands allows you to ask islanders to complete tasks. If you just take measurements on your participants, then it's an *observational study*. But if you also introduce something that's meant to change the outcome of a measurement (e.g., drinking coffee before taking a test), that's called an *experimental study*. You need to decide whether your study is observational or experimental.

- Observation

#### Question / Hypothesis

- How does the size of town someone lives in affect their job satisfaction?

#### Sampling plan

- (What steps will you take to collect the data?)
  - We are going to collect a random sample of 68 houses in the two smallest and two largest villages.
  - Each team member is assigned one village.
  - First, every house was assigned a number and then ordered randomly.
  - Second, the houses were sampled one by one.
  - At each house, a working member of the family was randomly chosen and surveyed.
  - The person was asked "Do you like your job?".
  - Even if a person elaborated beyond yes or no, only a 1 was recorded for no and a 3 for yes.
  - Non-working or people who declined were skipped and we moved to the next house.
  - This process was repeated until 68 samples were obtained.
  - Job satisfaction, job, age, name, salary, and town were recorded for each person surveyed.
- (How will you ensure the data is representative of your chosen population?)
  - Large sample size of 68 and random sampling which lowers our standard error and thus is more representative.
- (For experiments only: How will you ensure any effects you observe are due to the treatment, and not due to other factors?)
  - N/A
- (How will you choose your sample size?)
  - We went for a 90% confidence interval with a 10% margin of error which necessitates a sample size of 68. This was on the upper end of what was feasible time wise.

### **q2** EDA

Conduct an EDA on your data. Add as many code chunks as you need. Ensure your EDA gives enough context of the data for us to understand what comes next in this report.

```{r q2_data_pull}
filename_job <- "./data/c10-job-satistfaction-data.csv"
df_clean <- read_csv(filename_job)
df_jobs <- read_csv(filename_job) |> 
  mutate(Satisfied = if_else(Satisfied > 2, "Yes", "No")) 
  
df_jobs
```

```{r q2_eda}
ci_jobs <- df_jobs %>%
  group_by(Village) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    n_satisfied = sum(Satisfied == "Yes"),
    p = n_satisfied / n,
    SE = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n),
    ME = 1.645 * SE,
    lower_CI = p - ME,
    upper_CI = p + ME
  ) %>%
  select(Village, lower_CI, upper_CI, p)

ci_jobs

ci_jobs %>%
  ggplot(aes(Village, p, ymin = lower_CI, ymax = upper_CI, color = Village)) +
  geom_errorbar() +
  guides(color = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Village", y = "Percentage Satisfied", title = "Job Satisfaction  Percentage by Village (95% confidence interval)") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
  
df_jobs %>%
  ggplot(aes(Village, Income, color = Village)) +
  geom_boxplot() + 
  labs(title = "Income vs Village") +
  guides(color = FALSE) + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
  

df_jobs %>%
  ggplot(aes(Village, Age, color = Village)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Age vs Village") +
  guides(color = FALSE) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )

#adding labels for villages considered large/small
df_histogram <-
  df_clean %>%
  mutate(
    size_group = if_else(Village %in% c("Colmar", "Mahuti"), "large", "small")
  )


df_boot_prop <-
  df_histogram %>%
  bootstraps(., times = 1000) %>%
  mutate(
    diff_est = map_dbl(
      splits,
      function(split_df) {
        analysis(split_df) %>%
          summarize(
            diff_est = mean(Satisfied[size_group == "large"] == 3) -
              mean(Satisfied[size_group == "small"] == 3)
          ) %>%
          pull(diff_est)
      }
    )
  )

df_boot_prop %>%
  ggplot(aes(diff_est)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(
    x = "Estimated Difference",
    y = "Count",
    title = "Boostrap Difference Between Large and Small Town Job Satisfaction"
  )
```

### **q3** Key Analyses

Present the key analyses that support your questions / hypotheses. This could include summary statistics (e.g., a proportion of Islanders), grouped summary statistics (e.g., a proportion for group A, and for group B), or visualizations (e.g., a histogram). This section should be short, and every analysis should directly relate to q4.

We found that there was no correlation between the size of town someone lives in and their job satisfaction. As shown in graph 1 above, the 95% confidence intervals overlap for all four towns meaning we cannot be confident there is a real difference in job satisfaction. We also made plots of our covariats (Age and Income) and there was still no perceptible difference. This signals that job satisfaction is driven by factors other than what we were looking for. Finally, we also ran a bootstrap analysis and found there may be a slightly higher satisfaction for people in larger villages but it was not statistically significant.

### **q4** Answers

Connect your Key Analyses to your questions / hypotheses. What did you conclude from your study?

We concluded that at a 90% confidence interval there is no statistical difference between the size of town in which someone lives and their job satisfaction.
